catalog_quote: [Willis 2009 sec. 2.1.6] Late Brythonic had penultimate stress, which became word-final stress as the result of the loss of word-final syllables. In Old Welsh, the stress accent shifted back to the penultimate syllable, although the pitch accent remained word-final, resulting in the dissociation of stress and pitch accent characteristic of Welsh today. ... The date of the accent shift has been the subject of dispute. Morris-Jones (1913: 48) thought it occurred in early Middle Welsh (twelfth to early thirteenth century). Conversely, Watkins (1972, 1976) considers it to have occurred much earlier than this, perhaps in the ninth century ... This supports an Old Welsh (ninth-century) date for the accent shift. [Morris-Jones 1913 sec. 39 i] In a polysyllabic word, one syllable is always pronounced with more emphasis than the others ... In Welsh the accent is a stress accent. [sec. 40] i. In …

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations were re-opened in the copies we hold and match verbatim at the stated sections/pages (one silently dropped sentence in the Willis excerpt, no change of sense). The classification (MW penultimate stress, right edge, weight-blind; earlier OW final stress noted in the secondary-stress rule; listed exceptions from Morris-Jones sec. 41) rests on a 2009 specialist chapter with a dedicated stress section plus the standard 1913 historical grammar, and is uncontroversial in the field. Two Glottolog-listed grammars downloaded now (Evans 1964 GMW, Falileyev 2008) either presuppose penult accent or defer the topic; neither contradicts. Remaining unheld works (Jackson 1953, Watkins 1972, Schrijver 1995) bear only on the dating of the OW accent shift, already represented in the secondary-stress rule, so no reclassification or re-read is needed.

sources.quote: No dedicated accent section; penultimate accent is presupposed: sec. 2 '[MW u] persisted longer in accented syllables (including monosyllabic words) than in unaccented finals'; sec. 5 'final unaccented syllables'; Addenda p. 267 'in certain positions, e.g. the accented penult, as in [axel] uchel'. Consistent with penultimate word stress in MW polysyllables.
sources.locator: sec. 2 pp. 1-2; Addenda p. 267 (to p. 2 sec. 2)

sources.quote: Only mentions accent in the vowel-quantity rule ('Elles sont semi-longues sous l'accent dans les polysyllabes'); position of the Old Welsh accent is not stated -- n. 16 explicitly defers: 'Sur l'orthographe des textes vieux-gallois et l'accentuation en vieux-gallois, voir la bibliographie dans Falileyev (2000).' No section on accent placement.
